title: Where Do Right and Wrong Even Come From?
excerpt: Almost everyone believes some things are really wrong and not just unpopular, and that belief is harder to account for than most people admit.
body:
Start with something you already believe. Torturing a child for fun is wrong. Not wrong-for-you, not wrong-in-our-culture, not wrong-because-we-voted-on-it. Wrong. If a society passed a law approving it, the law would be evil and the society would be mistaken, and you know this with a confidence that survives every argument anyone has ever made against it.

That conviction is the thing we have to account for. Where does it come from, and what does it tell us about the world?

## The Skeptic's Case at Full Strength

Let me state the skeptic's case at full strength, because it is a serious case and I held it myself for years. The hardest version goes like this. Human beings are animals shaped by evolution. Creatures that cooperated survived and passed on their genes, so we inherited strong instincts to protect our own, to punish cheaters, to feel disgust at certain acts. What we call morality is the felt residue of those instincts plus thousands of years of cultural negotiation. It feels like we are perceiving a real moral law. We are actually feeling a very deep preference. There is no law out there. There is only the wiring in here, and the wiring is what natural selection found useful.

Notice what this account gets right, because it gets a great deal right. Evolution surely did shape our moral emotions. Cultures do differ on a thousand things. People do dress up self-interest as principle constantly, and a theory that explains how we came to feel moral feelings is doing real work. None of that is in dispute. Francis Collins, who led the mapping of the human genome and was an atheist into adulthood, grants every bit of the biology. He simply noticed that the biology does not reach the thing it was asked to explain.

Here is the gap. An account of how we came to have a belief is not an account of whether the belief is true. Suppose I tell you exactly why you believe two and two make four, tracing it to brain chemistry and childhood and the survival value of counting. I have explained the belief. I have said nothing about whether two and two actually make four. They do, and they would whether or not any creature ever evolved to notice it. The origin story of a belief and the truth of a belief are two different questions, and the evolutionary account answers only the first.

## The Gap Between Origin and Truth

> An account of how we came to have a belief is not an account of whether the belief is true.

So press the second question. When you say torturing a child for fun is wrong, are you reporting a fact about the act, or are you reporting a fact about your feelings? Everything turns on this. If you are only reporting your feelings, then a person with different feelings is not mistaken, only different, the way someone who dislikes cilantro is not mistaken. But that is not what you mean. You do not mean that you happen to dislike child-torture. You mean it would be wrong even if every human being on earth came to enjoy it. You are making a claim about the act, not about your appetite.

This is the moral argument, and C.S. Lewis put its starting point better than anyone. He noticed that people quarreling do not say I do not like what you did. They say that is not fair, you promised, give me my share. They appeal to a standard they expect the other person to recognize, and the other person almost never replies that there is no such standard. He argues that he did not really break it. Both parties are reaching for a law above them both, the way two men measuring a board reach for a ruler neither of them invented.

## The Reformer Who Stood Against His Society

The skeptic can answer here, and the answer deserves respect. He can say the standard is real but it is built by us, a contract we make so we can live together, refined over centuries the way law is refined. There is genuine wisdom in this. Much of our actual moral progress does look like negotiation and revision. But the contract account has a hard edge it cannot get past. If right and wrong are only agreements among the powerful, then the reformer who stands against his entire society has no ground to stand on. When abolitionists said slavery was wrong while their whole legal order said it was lawful, they were not proposing a better contract. They were saying the contract itself was evil, measured against something higher than the contract. If morality is only the agreement, the people who broke the agreement to free slaves were simply criminals, and we know they were not. We know they saw something true that their society was blind to. That knowledge requires a standard above every society, the very thing the contract account denies.

It is worth slowing down here, because the contract account is the most respectable secular answer and it keeps coming back in new clothes. Some say morality is what maximizes well-being, the greatest good for the greatest number. Others say it is what a fully rational and impartial person would choose. These are serious proposals and they capture real wisdom about how to weigh competing goods. But every one of them smuggles in a value it cannot justify on its own terms. Why should I care about the greatest good for the greatest number rather than the greatest good for me and mine? Why should I be impartial when partiality so often serves me better? The proposals tell you how to pursue the good once you have already agreed that you ought to. They do not tell you why you ought to, and that ought is the whole mystery. You can build an elaborate machine for calculating the right thing to do and still have said nothing about why the right thing makes a claim on you that you are not free to ignore. The machinery assumes the obligation it was supposed to explain.

There is a sharper way to feel this. Imagine the last truly evil thing you heard about, the headline that made your stomach turn. Now ask what you were actually doing in that moment of revulsion. You were not consulting a contract. You were not running a calculation about social utility. You were perceiving something, the way you perceive that a room is cold or a note is flat, except that what you perceived was a quality of wrongness in the act itself, a wrongness that seemed to be there independent of you, that you discovered rather than invented. That is the raw datum, and any theory of morality has to either explain it or explain it away. The theories that explain it away are tidy. They are also unlivable, because the very people who hold them go on perceiving wrongness as a feature of the world the moment they stop philosophizing and start living.

## When a Fact Becomes a Command

There is a second pressure point, quieter and harder. Suppose you accept that objective moral facts exist, hanging there in reality the way mathematical facts do. You still have to explain why those facts would have any authority over you. A mathematical fact does not command me. It does not lay an obligation on my will. But moral facts do exactly that. They do not merely describe. They oblige. They say you must, and they hold you guilty when you do not. A bare fact floating in the structure of the universe cannot issue a command, because commands come from persons. The strange and stubborn feature of moral experience is that it feels less like seeing a fact and more like hearing a voice, a summons that is over us and addressed to us. That feature is hard to explain on any view where the universe is, at bottom, impersonal stuff.

> The strange and stubborn feature of moral experience is that it feels less like seeing a fact and more like hearing a voice, a summons that is over us and addressed to us.

This is where the Christian claim earns a hearing. Not because believers are better at being good, they plainly are not, but because the Christian account fits the shape of the experience. If the deepest thing in reality is not stuff but a person, a God whose own character is the standard of good, then moral facts are not free-floating after all. They are grounded in someone, which is why they can command. The voice you seem to hear is a voice. The obligation you feel is owed to someone. The guilt that follows wrongdoing is not a malfunction to be medicated away but an accurate signal that you have wronged not just a neighbor but the One whose image the neighbor bears.

## Where the Christian Claim Earns a Hearing

It is worth pausing on why this fit matters, because the skeptic can grant the fit and still shrug. Lots of stories fit the data, he might say, and fitting is cheap. True enough. But notice what the Christian account does not have to do, which is the thing the secular accounts cannot avoid doing. It does not have to pretend that your sense of obligation is an illusion while asking you to keep obeying it. It does not have to call your moral perceptions a useful trick of the genes and then trust those same perceptions to guide your life. It takes the data at face value. There really is a law. It really does oblige you. The guilt you feel when you break it is really tracking something. On the Christian account, every part of the moral experience is exactly what it presents itself as, which is a strong mark in favor of a theory, that it does not have to explain away the very thing it set out to explain.

Be careful here, because Christians overplay this and skeptics rightly call the foul. The argument does not say atheists cannot be good. They obviously can, often better than the religious, and any honest believer has been outclassed in kindness by people who believe nothing. The argument also does not say you need to believe in God to know right from wrong. You do not. A person can read the ruler perfectly while denying that any ruler exists. The claim is narrower and harder to escape. It is that the moral law you already obey, the one you reach for the instant someone wrongs you, makes more sense if it comes from somewhere than if it comes from nowhere. The atheist who lives by it is borrowing furniture from a house he says was never built.

## The House He Says Was Never Built

There is one more move worth naming, because it is the most honest one a skeptic can make, and I respect it more than the others. He can simply accept the cost. He can say, with the philosophers who followed this thought to its end, that if there is no God then there really is no objective right and wrong, that our moral convictions are a beautiful and useful illusion, and that we should keep them for the sake of getting along while admitting they point at nothing. This is consistent. It is also nearly impossible to live. The same person who says morality is an illusion will be outraged within the hour at genuine injustice, and the outrage will not feel like a preference. It will feel like a perception of something real. We are built, it seems, to bump into a moral floor that our theories tell us is not there.

> The atheist who lives by it is borrowing furniture from a house he says was never built.

So here is where this leaves you, and I am not going to tie it off neatly. You believe, as surely as you believe anything, that some things are truly wrong. That belief is either tracking something real or it is a useful trick your genes are playing. If it is a trick, you will go on living as though it is not, because you cannot do otherwise. And if it is real, then it is the kind of thing that has to come from somewhere, and the somewhere has to be the kind of thing that can issue a command. A law over us, addressed to us, that we did not make and cannot repeal. That has a name. The question is not whether you feel the law. You do. The question is who is speaking.

title: If God Is Real, Why Does He Feel So Hidden?
excerpt: If God wanted to be known, it seems He could simply show Himself, and His silence is one of the heaviest reasons people stop believing.
body:
There is a kind of doubt that arguments do not touch, because it is not really an argument. It is an ache. You have prayed into a ceiling. You have asked, honestly and without games, for some sign that anyone was listening, and what came back was the sound of your own breathing. If there is a God who loves you, why is the most important person in the universe also the most absent?

## The Argument Hiding Inside the Ache

Let me put the skeptic's version of this in its strongest form, because there is a real argument hiding inside the ache, and it is one of the best arguments against God anyone has made. The philosopher J.L. Schellenberg laid it out cleanly. If a perfectly loving God exists, He would want a relationship with every person able to have one. A relationship requires that you at least believe the other party exists. So a loving God would make sure that everyone open to Him believed He was there. But there are people, sincere, searching, not hardened, who do not believe He is there. Therefore, the argument concludes, a perfectly loving God does not exist. The hiddenness is not just sad. It is evidence.

Notice what is right about this. The premise that love seeks to be known is true. Parents do not hide from children they love. The honest searcher is real, and pretending he does not exist, or that everyone who fails to believe is secretly running from God, is both false and cruel. Some people genuinely look and do not find, and any answer that begins by calling them liars has already failed. So we have to take the argument on its own terms. Why would a loving God allow even the honest seeker to walk in the dark?

## How Long, O Lord

The first thing to say is that the Bible does not treat hiddenness as a strange exception. It treats it as a recurring feature of life with God, and it gives it a name. The Psalms are full of it. How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. Why do you hide your face. Almost half the Psalms are complaints, many of them addressed to a God who seems to have stepped out of the room. Whoever wrote and kept and prayed these did not believe that God's felt absence disproved Him. They believed it was part of the relationship, painful and real, and they kept talking into it. That does not solve the problem. But it tells you that the experience you are having is not evidence that you are doing faith wrong. It is the experience the book itself describes.

## What Kind of Knowing Love Aims At

> The fear of an obvious king is not the love of a hidden father.

Now to the argument's machinery. The weak link is the assumption about what kind of knowing a loving God would aim at. Schellenberg assumes that love wants belief, the bare cognitive fact that someone exists. But that is not the deepest thing love wants. Love wants love in return, freely given, and freely given love needs room that overwhelming proof would crush. Consider a powerful man who wants to know whether a woman loves him for himself. If he announces his fortune, he will get plenty of devotion and never know what any of it is worth, because the proof of his wealth has made free love impossible. He has to stay partly hidden to be loved truly. This is not a perfect parallel, but it points at something real. A God who flooded every mind with undeniable proof of His existence and power would secure belief and might make love harder, because the response would be compelled. The fear of an obvious king is not the love of a hidden father.

Pascal saw this and put it with his usual edge. He said that God has given enough light for those who desire to see, and enough darkness for those who desire the opposite. The evidence is calibrated not to coerce. There is enough to find if you want Him and enough room to dismiss if you do not, and that arrangement is exactly what you would expect if God valued your freedom more than your certainty. The skeptic hears this and reasonably objects that it sounds too convenient, an excuse that explains away the absence by calling it a feature. The objection has teeth. But notice that it cuts both ways. If God did make Himself overwhelmingly obvious, the same skeptic could rightly complain that he was being bullied into belief by a cosmic show of force, his freedom run over. There may be no amount of evidence that satisfies both demands at once, which suggests the demands themselves are in tension, not that God has failed a test.

## Faith as a Relationship That Grows

There is another angle worth holding up, because the bare argument treats faith as a single moment, a yes or no flipped once and settled. But that is not how knowing a person works, and the Bible never describes it that way. Knowing God is portrayed as something that grows, that has seasons, that deepens through trust extended over time and tested in the dark. If that is the kind of knowing on offer, then a relationship that began with overwhelming proof would not be the same kind of thing at all. It would be more like knowing a fact than knowing a person. The hiddenness, on this reading, is not God withholding Himself from a relationship. It is the texture of a real relationship with a God who will not be reduced to a proven proposition, who wants to be trusted and not merely conceded. Trust, by its nature, operates where sight runs out. A God who left no room for trust would have left no room for the very thing He was after.

This still does not reach the honest seeker who is not playing games and simply finds the room empty, and I do not want to lose that person in the machinery. So let me say plainly that the experience of seeking and not finding is not, by itself, a sign of failure or of secret resistance. The Bible holds out a promise that those who seek will find, but it never promises the finding will be quick, or that the seeking will feel like anything but darkness while it lasts. Some of the people who knew God most deeply reported long stretches of nothing, years of it, dryness that did not lift on schedule. They called it a normal part of the life of faith and not an exception to it. That is cold comfort in the middle of it, and I will not pretend otherwise. But it does mean that the silence you are in is described, anticipated, accounted for, rather than being the anomaly that breaks the whole picture.

## We Are Not the Neutral Observers We Imagine

There is a harder and more honest point underneath all this, and it is uncomfortable for everyone. We are not the neutral observers we imagine. The picture in the hiddenness argument is of a perfectly open seeker, hands clean, simply waiting for data. But no human being is actually neutral about whether there is a God to whom he is accountable. We have enormous stakes in the answer. If God is real, then I am not my own, my life is not mine to define, and there is someone I have wronged. That is not a neutral proposition. It is one most of us, in some chamber of the heart, would prefer to be false. The Bible's claim, blunt and unflattering, is that the problem is not only in the evidence but in us, that we are tilted, that we suppress what we do not want to see. This is hard to hear and easy to abuse, and I will not pretend every doubter is secretly hiding. But honesty requires admitting that none of us comes to this question from nowhere.

## The God Who Entered the Silence

> Whatever Christianity says about the silence of God, it does not say it from a safe distance.

Still, set all the arguments aside, because they do not reach the ache, and the ache is the real subject. Here is the strangest fact about Christianity, the one that makes it different from a philosophy of the hidden God. At the center of the faith is a man crying out from a cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. That is the voice of hiddenness, and it is on the lips of God's own Son. Whatever Christianity says about the silence of God, it does not say it from a safe distance. It says that God Himself entered the silence, took the full weight of the absence, and cried the very words the doubter cries. The God of this faith is not a stranger to abandonment. He has been there, at the bottom of it, in the dark.

It is worth sitting with how strange this is compared to every other account of the hidden God. The deist imagines a God who set the world running and stepped back, indifferent to the silence because He was never near. The philosopher imagines a God so far above us that our cries do not register, the silence a sign of distance. Christianity says something no other view dares to say, that the highest God came the whole way down, took the silence into His own throat, and screamed it. The hiddenness is not a sign that God is far. It is a thing God Himself has tasted. Whatever your darkness is, He has stood in a darker one, and He stood in it for you. That does not switch the lights on. But it changes who is in the room.

> A God you can shout at in the dark is a strange kind of absent.

That does not explain the silence. I want to be careful not to hand you a neat resolution, because there is not one. People who walk with God for fifty years still go through long stretches where the line seems dead, and they are not doing it wrong. What the cross offers is not an explanation but a presence inside the experience, the claim that the silence you are in is not empty, that Someone has been in it before you and is in it with you, even when you cannot feel Him there. C.S. Lewis, after his wife died, wrote that the worst part was not doubting God's existence but fearing the truth about Him, that when you are happy you feel welcomed at His door, and when you are desperate you find it shut, bolted, and a sound of going away inside. He kept knocking anyway. Months later he wrote that the door had not opened so much as the frantic need to bang on it had quieted, and only then could he hear.

So I will leave you where the Psalms leave their readers, which is not in resolution. The hiddenness is real. It is not proof of His absence, but it is not nothing either, and you are allowed to say so out loud, to Him, in the words the Psalms already wrote for you. How long. Why do you hide your face. The remarkable thing is not that the Bible has no good answer to those questions. The remarkable thing is that it puts the questions in your mouth and tells you to keep asking. A God you can shout at in the dark is a strange kind of absent. The seeking is not the proof that He is gone. It may be the early sign that He is drawing you.

title: How Can a Loving God Send Anyone to Hell?
excerpt: The doctrine of hell strikes most people as the cruelest thing Christianity teaches, and the objection deserves a real answer rather than a flinch.
body:
Of everything Christianity asks people to believe, hell is the teaching that makes them want to leave the room. It is not merely hard. It seems monstrous. A God of infinite love, we are told, will consign people to infinite torment for finite sins committed in a few short decades, often by people who never had a fair chance. Stated that way, it is not a doctrine you defend. It is a doctrine you flee. And I want to begin by saying that if that statement were an accurate account of what the faith teaches, fleeing would be the right response.

## The Objection at Its Full Force

Let me give the objection its full force, because it has several parts and each one bites. First, the punishment seems wildly out of proportion. No human court would torture a thief forever, yet hell is endless. Second, it seems to make God into something worse than the cruelest tyrant, a being who creates conscious creatures knowing He will torment most of them without end. Third, it seems to corrupt the believer, because anyone who can be at peace in heaven while others scream below has had something human burned out of him. These are not cheap shots. The most serious people who have left the faith often point here, and they are not being shallow. They are being moral. The objection is, at its root, a moral protest, and that should make a Christian listen rather than argue, because the protest is reaching for something true.

Now let me try to say what the doctrine actually is, because much of the horror attaches to a cartoon. Start with the protest itself. When you recoil at the idea of injustice done to the undeserving, you are appealing to a standard of justice. You are saying some things are so wrong that they must be answered, that a universe where evil is simply shrugged off would be intolerable. Hold onto that, because it is the very intuition the doctrine of judgment is built on. A God who looked at genocide, at the trafficking of children, at a lifetime of cruelty, and felt nothing, did nothing, let it all evaporate into nothing at death, would not be loving. He would be morally asleep. The same heart that protests hell also protests a God who would not judge at all. We want evil answered. Judgment is the name for evil being answered. The question is not whether there should be justice. The question is what its shape and limits are.

## Borrowing the Faith's Own Ledger

Before going further, sit with how unusual it is that we even have this objection. The complaint that endless punishment is disproportionate assumes a scale of justice in which punishments should fit crimes, in which mercy is better than cruelty, in which the suffering of a person is a serious matter that the universe owes an accounting for. Where did that scale come from? Many cultures across history would have found the objection strange, would have shrugged at the suffering of the conquered or the low-born as simply the way of things. The conviction that every person's fate matters infinitely, that justice must be proportionate, that cruelty is an offense against the order of reality, is not the universal default. It is, to a remarkable degree, an inheritance from the very tradition being put on trial. The objector is borrowing the faith's own ledger to audit the faith's own books, which does not settle the question but should make us slow to assume the objection floats free of everything Christianity taught the world to value.

## The Gravity of the One Wronged

So consider the nature of the offense, the proportion problem. The usual picture is of God punishing trivial sins with infinite severity, and if sin were trivial the objection would stand. But the Christian claim is that sin is not first a matter of breaking rules. It is the rupture of a relationship with the source of all life and goodness, a turning away from the One in whom everything holds together. The gravity of a wrong is measured partly by the one wronged. Tear a stranger's photograph and it is rude. Tear your mother's only photograph of her dead son and you have done something far heavier, though the paper is the same. Sin against the infinite God is not infinite because we are important. It is grave because He is. That does not by itself prove the duration of hell, but it dissolves the cartoon of a cosmic overreaction to small things.

## Doors Locked on the Inside

> It describes hell as God, in the end, honoring the choice a person has spent a lifetime making, the choice to be his own god, to live without the real one.

Now the deeper move, the one Lewis made and Tim Keller after him, and the one that changes the whole picture. The most serious Christian thinking does not describe hell as God dragging unwilling people into a torture chamber. It describes hell as God, in the end, honoring the choice a person has spent a lifetime making, the choice to be his own god, to live without the real one. Lewis said the doors of hell are locked on the inside. He meant that hell is what the freedom to refuse God finally becomes when it is allowed to have its way forever. A person can spend a life narrowing inward, building a self that wants no master, and God will not, at the last, override that. He takes our freedom seriously enough to let it succeed. Hell, on this view, is not God refusing to let people out. It is God refusing to force people in. The gates are locked from within.

This reframes the objection without dodging it. The doubter pictures a person pounding on hell's door begging to be let into heaven while God laughs. That picture is not the historic teaching and not, I think, the reality. The far stranger and more sober claim is that the person in hell does not want what heaven is. Heaven is the unfiltered presence of the God he organized his entire existence around avoiding. To that self, heaven would be the torment. Keller put it sharply. He said hell is just one's freely chosen identity apart from God on a trajectory into infinity. We see the early version of this in ordinary life, the person who has chosen resentment for so long that he can no longer enjoy anyone's happiness, who would rather be right and alone than reconciled. Run that out forever. That is the warning.

## Judgment That Turns Back on You

The skeptic can press back, and the strongest counter deserves room. He can say this is too neat, that real people are mixtures, that almost no one is a pure refuser, that plenty of people would gladly take God if He were on offer in terms they could accept. This is fair, and it is why Christians have always insisted that judgment belongs to God alone and not to us, precisely because only He can read a human heart to its floor. We are spectacularly bad at it. We write people off who are not finished and excuse people who are. The doctrine of judgment is not a license to sort our neighbors into the saved and the damned. It is a warning aimed first at the one reading it. Whenever the New Testament talks about judgment, it almost never lets you apply it to someone else. It turns it back on you. Examine yourself.

There is a third part of the objection that deserves its own answer, the charge that the doctrine corrupts the believer, that anyone capable of enjoying heaven while others suffer has had his humanity burned out. This is the sharpest version and it has worried serious Christians too. But notice the assumption inside it, that the person in heaven would look down on the lost as strangers whose fate is no concern of his. That is not the Christian hope. The hope is of a people remade, more loving than they are now and not less, more pained by loss and not numbed to it. If anything, the redeemed would feel the tragedy of a refused God more keenly than we do, not less, the way a healed person feels the wrongness of sickness more sharply than the sick. The Christian does not look forward to a heaven where he has stopped caring. He looks forward to a justice and a mercy so complete that, when finally seen whole, it does not require him to stop caring in order to be at peace. How those two things meet is beyond what I can draw for you. But the cartoon of the smug saved gloating over the damned is a thing the faith condemns, not a thing it teaches.

## The Question of Endlessness

There is the matter of duration, the endlessness, which troubles many honest believers and not only skeptics. I will be candid that faithful Christians have held more than one view here, and Scripture is less explicit than the popular imagination assumes. Some read the language of destruction as meaning exactly that, that the finally unrepentant cease to be rather than suffer forever. Others hold the traditional view. The tradition has more room in it than the cartoon allows, and a person can take the warnings of judgment with full seriousness without committing to the most lurid version. What no faithful reading allows is the comfortable assumption that nothing is at stake, that all roads arrive at the same place and the choices of a life carry no final weight. The whole drama of the Bible insists that what you do with God matters, ultimately and forever. That is the hard floor under every softer reading.

## The God Who Walked Into the Dock

> A tyrant does not die for the people he is angry at.

And there is something the objection always leaves out, the thing that changes its entire register. The God who warns of judgment is the God who walked directly into it. The cross is the place where the One with every right to judge took the judgment Himself. Christianity does not teach a God who sits at a safe distance condemning the guilty. It teaches a God who came down into the dock, who absorbed in His own body the verdict we had earned, who did for us at infinite cost the one thing we could not do for ourselves. Whatever you make of hell, you cannot make of this God an indifferent tyrant. A tyrant does not die for the people he is angry at. The same Bible that speaks most about judgment shows you a God spreading His arms on a Roman cross and saying, in effect, let it fall on me instead.

So I will not end this with a bow, because the subject does not allow one. Hell remains the hardest thing the faith teaches, and anyone who discusses it lightly has not felt its weight. But I would ask you to notice where your protest against it actually comes from. It comes from a conviction that evil must be answered and that love must be real, and both of those convictions are not arguments against the Christian God. They are arguments toward Him. The faith takes evil seriously enough to say it will be answered, and it takes love seriously enough to say that God paid the answer Himself. What it will not do is tell you that your choices are weightless. They are not. That is the warning, and it is also, strangely, a kind of dignity. You matter enough that what you do with God is allowed to be final.

title: What About People Who Never Heard of Jesus?
excerpt: It seems deeply unfair that eternity could hinge on whether you happened to be born where the message reached, and the unfairness is worth facing squarely.
body:
Picture a woman who lived her whole life in a remote valley two thousand years before Christ, who never heard the name of Jesus and could not have, who was kind to her neighbors and grieved her dead and looked at the stars and wondered. If salvation comes only through faith in a man she had no possible way of hearing about, then her eternity was decided by an accident of geography and calendar. That seems not merely sad. It seems unjust on a scale that would call into question the goodness of any God who arranged it.

## Holding the Objection at Full Strength

This is one of the strongest objections to the Christian faith, and I want to resist the urge to make it small. The unfairness is real. A God who damned billions for failing a test they were never given the chance to take would be a moral monster, and no amount of theological footwork should be allowed to disguise that. So let us hold the objection at full strength and not flinch. Why would a loving and just God make eternal destiny depend on access to information that most human beings who ever lived did not have?

## Judged by the Light Actually Given

> The test is not did you hear the name. The test is what did you do with what reached you.

The first thing to say is that the Bible itself raises this question and does not treat it as a gotcha. Paul, writing to the Romans, asks how people can call on someone they have not heard of, and the honest pressure of that question is right there in the text. But the same Paul, a chapter earlier, says something the popular version of Christianity often forgets. He says that people who never had the written law will be judged by what they did with what they did have, that there is a law written on the human heart, that conscience accuses or excuses them. In other words, the Bible never says people are judged for failing to believe a message they never received. It says people are judged according to the light they were actually given. The test is not did you hear the name. The test is what did you do with what reached you.

This matters enormously, and it cuts against a crude picture many Christians carry and many skeptics assume Christians must hold. The crude picture is that God runs a pass or fail exam on a single question, and the question is have you said the right words about Jesus, and everyone who was out of earshot fails automatically. That is not what the historic faith teaches at its most careful. God judges justly, which means He judges each person by what was genuinely available to them, their light, their conscience, their response to the goodness and beauty and moral law they could actually perceive. No one is condemned for an ignorance they could not help. People are responsible for what they suppress, not for what they were never shown.

## Abraham, Who Was Saved Without the Name

Now, this raises an obvious follow-up, and the skeptic is right to ask it. If people can be judged by the light they have, and some respond to that light, are they saved without Jesus? Here Christians divide, and I will be honest about the disagreement rather than pretend there is one tidy answer. The clearest line in the New Testament is that salvation comes through Christ alone, that no one comes to the Father except through Him. But that is a claim about how salvation is accomplished, not necessarily a claim that a person must possess explicit information about the historical Jesus to benefit from what He did. Consider that the entire population of faithful Israel before Christ, Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets, never heard the name Jesus of Nazareth and never believed the specific facts of His death and resurrection, because those events had not happened yet. Yet the New Testament treats Abraham as the very model of saving faith. He was saved through Christ without knowing Christ's name, on the basis of trusting the God who had revealed Himself to him as far as that revelation went.

If that is true of those who lived before Christ, it is hard to see why it could not be true of those who lived after Him but outside the reach of the message, judged not by information they lacked but by their response to the God who was reaching toward them through everything they did have. This is a real position held by serious Christians, including thinkers like C.S. Lewis, who imagined that some who never knew the name might be turning, without knowing it, toward the One who bears it. It is not universalism. It does not say everyone is saved. It says that the basis of judgment is the heart's response to whatever light God gave, and that the One doing the judging knows that light perfectly in a way we never could.

## The Limits of Generosity

Let me name the limits honestly, because there is a temptation to make this so generous that it empties the message of any urgency. If everyone outside earshot is judged purely by general light and most do fine, then the missionary enterprise looks not just unnecessary but cruel, since hearing the name might only increase the chance of failing. There is a real tension here, and the New Testament holds both ends of it. It insists that God judges justly those who never heard, and it insists that the message is genuinely good news that people need to hear, that more light is mercy and not danger, that knowing the name and the face of God in Christ is a gift worth crossing the world to bring. The resolution is not that the unevangelized are fine and the message is optional. It is that God deals justly with each according to what they had, and that the fullest thing anyone can have is to actually know Him in Christ, and that this knowing is so good that withholding it would be the unkindness.

## A God Already Present and Reaching

It helps to see how old this question is, because the way the Bible handles it is not a modern patch applied under pressure. The earliest believers were Jews wrestling with exactly this. They had a God who had revealed Himself in a particular place, to a particular people, through a particular history, and they had to make sense of the rest of the world walking in less light. Their answer was not that God did not care about the nations. It was that God had been at work among them all along, that He had not left Himself without witness anywhere, that He sent rain and harvest and the moral sense to peoples who had never seen a prophet. Paul, standing in Athens among people who worshiped gods he thought were false, did not tell them they were beyond reach. He told them they had been groping for the true God in the dark, that He was not far from any one of them, that in Him they already lived and moved and had their being without knowing His name. That is a striking thing to say to pagans. It assumes a God already present and already reaching, in places the message had not yet come.

> The missionary does not bring God to a Godless place.

This reframes what we mean when we worry about the unevangelized. We tend to picture God as absent from the unreached valley until a missionary arrives to import Him, as though He were confined to the places where the message had spread. But the Bible's picture is of a God already there, already speaking through conscience and creation and the hunger for meaning that shows up in every human culture, already drawing people who have never heard a sermon. The missionary does not bring God to a Godless place. He brings the name and the face to a place where God has been working in shadow all along. That does not answer every question about how God deals with each soul. But it dissolves the picture of an absentee deity who damns by default everywhere the mail has not yet reached.

## On What Basis Would God Include Any of Us

> The astonishing thing in the Christian story is not that some are judged. It is that anyone is rescued.

There is a deeper assumption inside the objection worth surfacing, because it quietly drives the whole thing. The objection assumes that the default destiny of a human being is heaven, and that God is looking for reasons to exclude people, so that anyone who lacks the entry code gets shut out. But the Christian picture is closer to the reverse. It is not that innocent people are being denied admission on a technicality. It is that all of us, in every valley and every century, have turned from the God we did know, suppressed the light we did have, wronged the neighbors we could see. The astonishing thing in the Christian story is not that some are judged. It is that anyone is rescued. The question is not why would God exclude the woman in the valley. The question is on what basis would God include any of us, and the answer the faith gives is the same for her as for you, the costly mercy of God reaching toward people who had turned away.

## Shall Not the Judge of All the Earth Do Right

The skeptic can still press, and the sharpest form of the press is this. Even granting all of the above, why would God set up a world where the message spreads so unevenly, where some are born flooded with light and others in shadow? Why not reveal Himself equally to all? And here I have to be honest that we reach the edge of what anyone can answer. I do not know why the history of revelation runs the way it does, why some eras and places received more and others less. The Bible does not fully tell us. What it tells us is the character of the Judge, that He is just, that He shows no partiality, that He will do right by every person in a way that, when all is finally seen, will satisfy rather than offend the deepest moral sense in us, the very sense that makes us protest now.

So I will leave it there, unfinished, because finishing it would require knowing things I do not. What I can say is that the objection, taken to the bottom, is an objection rooted in a passion for fairness, and that passion is not a reason to reject the Christian God. It is something the Christian God shares. Abraham, standing before God, asked the question that every honest doubter is really asking. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right. He asked it not as an accusation but as a confidence, and the whole Bible is an answer in the affirmative. You may not get, on this side of things, the full account of how God deals with every soul in every shadowed valley. What you are offered is the character of the one who decides, and the invitation to trust that He will be more just, and more merciful, than you in your love of justice would dare to demand.

title: Hasn't the Church Done Terrible Things?
excerpt: The crimes committed under the banner of Christ are real and many, and any honest defense of the faith has to own them before it says anything else.
body:
I am not going to begin this by minimizing anything, because the minimizing is part of the offense. The church has blessed slave ships. It has burned dissenters. It has run residential schools that stripped children of their language and their families, sometimes their lives. It has covered for men who abused children and moved them to fresh parishes to abuse again. It has baptized empire, justified conquest, and called the spoils a mission. These are not slanders invented by the faith's enemies. They are facts, many of them documented by the church's own records, and a Christianity that cannot say so plainly is not worth defending.

## Look at the Fruit, Judge the Tree

The objection built on this is simple and devastating. If Christianity were true, if it actually changed people and connected them to a holy God, you would expect its followers to be conspicuously better than everyone else. Instead they have often been worse, or at least no better, and sometimes the institution itself has been the engine of the cruelty. So either the faith does not do what it claims, or the claim is false. Look at the fruit, the objection says, and judge the tree.

That is a serious argument and it has a true premise inside it. Jesus Himself said you will know them by their fruit. He invited exactly this scrutiny. So the question is not whether the church's crimes count against it. They do, and a believer who waves them away has not understood his own scriptures. The question is what, precisely, they count against, and whether they count against the thing the faith actually claims or against a thing it does not claim.

## A Hospital, Not a Museum

> The church is, by its own description, a hospital for the morally sick, not a museum of the morally finished.

Start with the most important and least comfortable point. Christianity is the one major worldview whose own founding documents predict and explain exactly this failure. The faith does not teach that its followers are good people who have arrived. It teaches the opposite, that they are people who have admitted they are not good, who needed rescue precisely because they could not make themselves righteous. The church is, by its own description, a hospital for the morally sick, not a museum of the morally finished. So when you find sin inside it, you have not found a contradiction of the message. You have found the message confirmed in the ugliest possible way. The men who ran the inquisitions were not too Christian. By the standard their own book gives them, they were not Christian enough, and the book says so to their faces. Whatever Jesus taught, He did not teach men to burn heretics, and the verses they would have had to ignore to do it are not obscure.

## What Would Actually Count Against the Faith

Now, the skeptic can rightly object that this is too convenient. If good behavior proves the faith and bad behavior also proves the faith, since the faith predicted bad behavior, then nothing could ever count against it, and a theory that cannot be falsified is not telling you anything. This is a fair philosophical complaint and I do not want to slide past it. So let me name what would actually count against Christianity. It would count against the faith if Christianity produced no real saints, if it never moved anyone toward sacrificial love, if its teaching, faithfully followed, made people crueler. That is the test, and it is a test the faith can fail in principle. The honest comparison is not between Christians and angels. It is between what people did when they followed the teaching and what they did when they violated it. The Crusader killing in the name of Christ was disobeying Christ. The abolitionist freeing slaves in the name of Christ was obeying Him. Both quoted the same book. Only one was reading it rightly, and we can tell which, because the book is not actually ambiguous about whether you should massacre a city or whether you should love your enemy.

There is a sharper version of this worth stating, because skeptics sometimes reply that anyone can read anything they want out of a text, that the abolitionist and the slaveholder both found their case in the same book, so the book settles nothing. But this is not quite true, and the history shows it. The slaveholder had to work hard, had to lean on a handful of verses ripped from their setting and ignore the thundering arc of the whole story, a story that begins with a people freed from slavery and is organized around a God who hears the cry of the oppressed. The abolitionist did not have to strain. He had the grain of the thing running with him, the image of God in every person, the leveling truth that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. When two readers disagree and one has to suppress the central message to make his case while the other rides it, that is not a tie. It is a tell. The text is not infinitely pliable. It pushed, over centuries and against enormous economic interest, in one direction, and the people who finally won the argument won it with the book, not against it.

## The Other Half of the Ledger

This points to something the objection usually leaves out, which is the other half of the ledger. The same tradition that produced inquisitors also produced the people who built the first hospitals, who founded universities, who took in the infants left to die on Roman hillsides, who led the charge against the slave trade, who ran the underground railroad, who marched in Birmingham with scripture on their lips. The man who did more than any other to end the British slave trade, William Wilberforce, did it as an act of explicit Christian conviction, against a slaving establishment that was itself nominally Christian. The civil rights movement in America was not a secular movement that happened to use churches. It was a church movement, led by pastors, grounded in the claim that every person bears the image of God. You cannot tell the story of human rights without telling the story of people who got the idea that humans have inviolable worth from somewhere, and a great deal of that somewhere is the conviction that every person is made in the image of a God who loves them.

## Where the Measuring Stick Came From

There is a further point that the skeptic, to be consistent, has to face. The very standard by which we condemn the church's crimes is, in large part, a standard the church taught the world. When we say the Crusades were evil, that slavery was an abomination, that abusing the vulnerable is among the worst things a person can do, we are appealing to the dignity of the individual, the priority of the weak, the wrongness of using power to crush the powerless. Those are not the natural values of every culture and every age. The ancient world did not believe the weak had special claims. It believed the strong were entitled to rule the weak, and that exposing unwanted infants and crucifying slaves were simply how the world worked. The idea that the powerful owe something to the powerless, that the victim has moral priority over the conqueror, came into Western consciousness largely through a faith that worshiped a crucified victim. So when people use the language of the victim to condemn the church, they are often, without knowing it, using the church's own deepest teaching against the church's worst behavior. That is not a defense of the behavior. It is a clue about where the moral measuring stick came from.

> The capacity for monstrous evil is not located in religion. It is located in the human heart, and it will use whatever banner is available, the cross or the hammer or the flag or the race.

There is a comparison the objection usually avoids, and fairness requires making it, though carefully. The twentieth century ran a kind of experiment in what happens when societies deliberately threw off the Christian framework and built on something else. The regimes that set out to abolish religion and remake humanity on a purely material basis, in Russia and China and Cambodia, produced killing on a scale that dwarfs every religious atrocity in history combined, tens of millions dead in a few decades. I raise this not to score a point, because atheists did not kill in the name of atheism the way crusaders killed in the name of Christ, and the comparison can be abused. The honest lesson is narrower and more sobering for everyone. The capacity for monstrous evil is not located in religion. It is located in the human heart, and it will use whatever banner is available, the cross or the hammer or the flag or the race. The believer who thinks his faith makes him safe from it has not read his own scriptures, which say the line between good and evil runs through every human being, starting with him. Christianity does not claim to have found the good people. It claims to have diagnosed, more accurately than any rival, why there are no good people, and what it would cost to change that.

## The Wound That Is Real and Recent

But I do not want to let the faith off with a clever reversal, because the wound is real and recent. The abuse scandals are not medieval. They are the lifetime of people reading this. Institutions that should have protected children protected themselves instead, and did it while claiming the name of Christ, and the damage to faith those crimes caused is incalculable and largely deserved. There is no argument that heals that. The only honest response is the one the faith's own teaching demands, which is confession without excuse, repentance with restitution, and the recognition that judgment, as the New Testament says, begins with the household of God. A church that responds to its crimes with public relations rather than repentance has compounded the sin. The right Christian response to the church's evil is not defensiveness. It is grief, and the resolve to be different, and the willingness to say plainly that those who did these things in Christ's name betrayed Him.

So where does this leave the original objection. It leaves it true and incomplete. True, because the church really has done terrible things and a faith that denies it is lying. Incomplete, because the terrible things are violations of the faith's own teaching, not expressions of it, and because the same faith has produced an enormous amount of the world's mercy, and because the standard we use to judge the crimes was substantially shaped by the faith we are judging. The fruit is mixed because the field is mixed, because the church is full of unfinished people, and the faith said so from the start.

## The Question I Would Put Back

> The hypocrisy of Christians is real. It is also, oddly, a backhanded testimony to the height of the thing they failed to reach.

There is a question I would put back to the honest skeptic, not as a trap but because it is the question that turned me when I was outside all of this. Suppose you cleared away every false believer, every hypocrite, every institution that used Christ as a cover for power. Suppose you got down to the actual teaching and the actual man at the center of it. Would the problem be that He asks too little of you, or too much. The complaint against the church is almost always that it failed to live up to its founder. That is a strange complaint to make against a religion, and a revealing one. We do not usually fault a movement for falling short of a standard we think is worthless. We fault it for falling short of a standard we suspect, somewhere in us, is true. The hypocrisy of Christians is real. It is also, oddly, a backhanded testimony to the height of the thing they failed to reach.

title: Can a Reasonable Person Believe in Miracles?
excerpt: Modern people are taught that miracles are the one thing an educated person cannot accept, and that confidence rests on an argument worth examining.
body:
There is a feeling, deep in the modern mind, that the question of miracles was settled long ago, that science closed the door and grown-ups walked through it. People do not rise from the dead. Water does not turn to wine. We know how the world works now, and the world does not work like that. To believe otherwise is to believe in a flat earth, a charming relic from before we knew better. This feeling is so widespread that it usually does not present itself as an argument at all. It presents itself as maturity.

## Hume's Argument at Full Strength

But there is a real argument underneath the feeling, and it is worth stating at full strength, because it is a good one. The philosopher David Hume gave it its classic form in the eighteenth century, and it still does most of the work even for people who have never read him. A miracle, Hume said, is a violation of the laws of nature. The laws of nature are established by the most uniform and constant experience there is, billions of observations with no exception. The evidence for any reported miracle, by contrast, is some human testimony, and human testimony is notoriously unreliable, full of error, exaggeration, wishful thinking, and lies. So whenever you weigh a miracle report, you are weighing the most solid evidence imaginable, the uniform laws of nature, against the flimsiest, a few people's say-so. The wise man, Hume concluded, proportions his belief to the evidence, and the evidence will always favor the natural explanation. It is always more likely that the witnesses were mistaken than that the dead rose.

Notice how much of this is right, because it is mostly right. Human testimony is unreliable. People do exaggerate and deceive and see what they want to see. Most miracle reports, examined closely, do dissolve into rumor or fraud or honest mistake, and a healthy skepticism toward them is not arrogance but good sense. If a man tells you his uncle came back from the dead last Tuesday, you are right to doubt him, and you would be foolish to do otherwise. Hume is correct that extraordinary claims call for proportionate scrutiny. The error is not in the caution. The error is somewhere more subtle.

## The Circle in the Definition of Law

Here is the first crack. Hume's argument quietly defines the laws of nature as having no exceptions, and then uses that definition to rule out any reported exception in advance. But that is reasoning in a circle. The whole question is whether an exception has ever occurred. If you build the impossibility of exceptions into your definition of the laws, you have not discovered that miracles do not happen. You have assumed it before looking. The laws of nature describe what happens when nature is left to itself. They are descriptions of the regular pattern, the default behavior of matter. They are not laws in the sense of legislation that forbids anything. The law that dropped objects fall does not forbid me from catching a falling cup. My hand is not a violation of gravity. It is a new factor introduced into the situation. The question of miracles is exactly whether there is anyone outside the system who can introduce a new factor, the way my hand interrupts the fall of the cup without breaking any law of physics.

## Whether Miracles Are Possible Depends on God

> The author of a story is bound by its rules only as long as he chooses to be.

This is where the whole debate turns, and it turns on something that comes before the evidence. Whether miracles are possible depends entirely on whether God exists. If there is no God, if the physical universe is all there is and it runs as a closed system, then of course there are no miracles, because there is no one outside the machine to reach in. But if there is a God who made the regularities in the first place, then the regularities are not a cage that binds Him. They are His ordinary way of working, and there is no reason in principle He could not, on rare and meaningful occasions, do something else. The author of a story is bound by its rules only as long as he chooses to be. So the real question is never simply is this miracle report credible in isolation. It is also is there a God who might act, and what you already believe about that determines how you will read every report before you read it.

## The Method That Forbids the Genuinely New

> A method that forbids you ever to believe the genuinely new is not a method for finding truth. It is a method for protecting what you already think.

There is a further weakness in Hume's argument that later thinkers pressed hard, and it is worth seeing because it shows the reasoning proves too much. Hume says we should always reject the miracle because uniform experience stands against it. But uniform experience is exactly what is in dispute. To say experience is uniformly against miracles, you would have to know in advance that every reported miracle in history was false, which is the very thing you are trying to establish. You cannot use the claim no miracle has ever happened as evidence that this particular miracle did not happen, because the first claim is just the conclusion stated early. And there is a stranger problem. By Hume's logic, you should reject any sufficiently unprecedented event, no matter how good the testimony, simply because it is unprecedented. But science advances precisely by accepting well-attested events that overturn what uniform experience had suggested. If researchers had reasoned like Hume, they would have rejected every anomaly that did not fit the existing pattern, and the anomalies are often where the truth was hiding. A method that forbids you ever to believe the genuinely new is not a method for finding truth. It is a method for protecting what you already think.

This exposes something uncomfortable about the confident modern dismissal. It often presents itself as following the evidence, but it is frequently doing the reverse. It begins with the assumption that the universe is a closed system, that nothing outside nature exists or acts, and then it concludes that miracles cannot happen. But that assumption, philosophical naturalism, is not a discovery of science. Science studies the regular workings of nature, which is exactly what it should do, and it has nothing to say about whether anything exists beyond nature. The leap from science describes the regular pattern to nothing ever breaks the pattern is a philosophical leap, not a scientific finding, and it is usually made without notice. The person who says a reasonable man cannot believe in miracles has often smuggled in the conclusion at the start.

## The One Miracle on Which Everything Hangs

Now take the case the whole question really hangs on, because Christianity does not ask you to believe in miracles in general. It asks you to believe in one in particular, on which it stakes everything. Paul wrote that if Christ has not been raised, the entire faith is worthless and Christians are to be pitied. He did not hedge. He bet the farm on a historical event. So examine that one. What actually has to be explained is a cluster of facts that even most skeptical historians grant. A man named Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate and died. His followers, devastated and scattered, within a few weeks were proclaiming in the very city where he was killed that they had seen him alive. They went from terrified hiders to public witnesses who would not stop talking even under threat of death. The movement exploded out of Jerusalem, where anyone could have produced the body and ended it in an afternoon, and no one did. Within a generation there were written accounts naming witnesses still alive.

## Explaining the Facts Without a Resurrection

> But people do not die for what they know to be a lie, and these people died for this.

The naturalist has to explain those facts without a resurrection, and he can try. Maybe they stole the body and lied. But people do not die for what they know to be a lie, and these people died for this. Maybe they hallucinated. But hallucinations are private, and the reports describe groups, meals, conversations, a man eating fish. Maybe the legend grew over centuries. But the core proclamation is too early for that, traceable to within a few years of the event, far too soon for myth to crystallize while eyewitnesses were still around to object. Each natural explanation has been offered, and each has serious trouble, and the honest historian, even the unbelieving one, usually ends by saying we know the early Christians sincerely believed they had seen him risen, and there it stops, because the historian as historian cannot say what caused the belief. N.T. Wright has argued at book length that the rise of the resurrection belief is itself a fact in need of explanation, and that no first-century Jew would have invented a single risen messiah out of thin air, because it fit nothing they expected. Something happened. The question is what.

This is the point. Belief in the resurrection is not a flight from evidence. It is one explanation among several for a real body of historical data, and it is not obviously the worst one. It looks impossible only if you have already decided, before examining anything, that the universe is closed and God cannot act. If you have decided that, then no evidence could ever be enough, because any natural explanation, however strained, will always beat a miracle by definition, which is exactly Hume's circle running again. But if you hold the question open, if you grant that there might be a God who could act, then the resurrection stops being absurd and becomes a hypothesis you weigh like any other, against the alternatives, on the evidence.

## Following the Evidence Past the Closed Door

It is worth being honest about what does and does not follow, because Christians sometimes oversell this. The historical case does not prove the resurrection the way a syllogism proves its conclusion. History does not deal in proof of that kind. What the historical case does is shift the burden. It establishes a body of facts, the death, the empty tomb, the transformed witnesses, the sudden explosion of a movement proclaiming a risen and crucified messiah in the teeth of every expectation, that demand some explanation. It then shows that the natural explanations on offer are strained, each one buying its naturalism at the price of ignoring part of the data. At that point the resurrection is no longer the desperate option. It is a live one, sitting on the table next to the others, and the only thing that automatically rules it out is the prior assumption that nothing outside nature can act. Strip that assumption away, hold the question genuinely open, and a thoughtful person can look at the evidence and conclude that the best explanation is the one the witnesses gave, that he was raised. That is not blind faith. That is following the evidence past the point where a closed mind had decided in advance it was not allowed to go.

So I will not tell you that you must believe Jesus rose. That is a larger step and it involves more than argument. What I will tell you is that the confident claim that a reasonable person simply cannot believe such a thing does not survive examination. It rests on a definition that assumes its own conclusion and on a philosophy of nature that pretends to be a finding of science when it is not. A reasonable person can certainly reject miracles. But he cannot do it on the cheap, by waving the word science and assuming the door is closed. The door is exactly what is in question. Whether anyone is on the other side of it is the oldest question there is, and it is still open, and the empty tomb is still sitting there, in the historical record, waiting for an explanation that you have not yet been given a reason to refuse.

title: Isn't Faith Just Believing Without Evidence?
excerpt: The popular definition of faith as belief without evidence is so common it feels obvious, and it happens to be wrong about what faith has always meant.
body:
There is a definition of faith that everybody seems to know. Faith is believing something without evidence, or worse, believing something in spite of the evidence. On this view, faith and reason are opposites. Reason follows the facts wherever they lead. Faith plants its flag and refuses to move no matter what the facts say. The more you believe without proof, the more faith you have, so that the highest faith would be believing the most absurd things on the least grounds. Stated this way, faith is not a virtue. It is a flaw, a willful blindness dressed up as devotion, and a thinking person should want no part of it.

## The Real Target Underneath the Objection

I want to take this seriously because it is held seriously, and because there is a real target underneath it. There are religious people who believe things for terrible reasons, who treat doubt as sin and questions as betrayal, who would rather close their eyes than examine a hard fact. That kind of faith exists and it deserves the criticism it gets. If that were all faith could be, I would be against it too. So the question is not whether bad faith exists. It plainly does. The question is whether the definition fairly describes what faith has actually meant in the tradition, or whether it is attacking a caricature.

## What the Word Does in Ordinary Life

> It is trust, grounded in evidence, extended into the unknown.

Start with what the word does in ordinary life, because faith is not a religious term that escaped into common use. It is a common term that religion also uses. When you say you have faith in your wife, you do not mean you believe she exists without evidence. You mean you trust her, and your trust is built on years of evidence, on a thousand kept promises and proven loyalties. Your faith in her is not the absence of reasons. It is what you do with the reasons you have. It is the act of committing yourself to someone you have good grounds to trust, in the places where proof runs out and you have to lean your weight on the relationship. That is what faith is. It is trust, grounded in evidence, extended into the unknown. It is not the opposite of reason. It is what reasonable people do with reasonable conclusions when those conclusions ask for commitment.

## How the Bible Uses the Word

This is exactly how the Bible uses the word, which surprises people who have only heard the popular definition. The biblical word for faith is the word for trust, the kind you place in a person. And the biblical writers do not present trust as a leap into the dark away from evidence. They present it as a response to evidence. When the gospel writers tell their stories, they keep pointing at things, at the empty tomb, at the witnesses, at the healings people saw with their own eyes. John says outright that he wrote his account so that you might believe, and he describes the things Jesus did as signs, evidence offered to the mind. The apostles in the book of Acts do not say believe because we tell you to. They argue. They reason in the synagogues. They appeal to events that happened in public, in recent memory, that their hearers could check. Whatever else this is, it is not a celebration of believing without grounds.

There is one verse the popular view always reaches for, the line about faith being the evidence of things not seen, and it is worth looking at because it says nearly the reverse of what it is quoted to say. Not seen does not mean unsupported. We believe in plenty of things we cannot see, including most of what science tells us about atoms and distant galaxies and the deep past, none of which we observe directly. We hold them on the basis of evidence that points beyond what our eyes take in. And notice the word the verse uses for faith. It calls faith the evidence of things not seen, the assurance, the substance. The verse is not contrasting faith with evidence. It is calling faith a kind of well-grounded confidence about realities beyond sight. The doubting Thomas story makes the same point in a way people misread. Jesus does not condemn Thomas for wanting evidence. He gives him the evidence, shows him the wounds, invites him to touch. The mild rebuke is only that Thomas could have trusted the testimony of people he had every reason to trust, the way we accept countless true things on reliable testimony every day rather than demanding to personally verify each one.

## Where the Popular Definition Came From

It is worth noticing where the popular definition of faith actually came from, because it did not come from the religious traditions it claims to describe. It was largely manufactured in the last century or so by people arguing against religion, who found it useful to define faith as belief without evidence precisely because, so defined, it is easy to defeat. But you do not get to assign your opponent his own worst position and then congratulate yourself for refuting it. If you ask what faith meant to the people who built the tradition, to Augustine and Anselm and Aquinas, you find something almost the opposite of the popular caricature. Anselm described his whole project as faith seeking understanding, the conviction that belief was the starting point of a search for reasons, not a substitute for them. Aquinas wrote thousands of pages of the most rigorous argument the medieval mind produced, because he took for granted that faith and reason were partners working the same territory. These were not men hiding from evidence. They were men who thought belief had work to do and reasons to give, and who gave them at exhausting length.

## Doubt Is Not the Opposite of Faith

> Doubt is what faith feels like from the inside when it is alive and honest, the friction of a trusting mind that still has questions.

There is a related confusion worth clearing, between faith and certainty. People often assume that to have faith is to have no doubts, that the believer is someone who has switched off the part of him that questions. But doubt is not the opposite of faith. The opposite of faith is indifference, the refusal to care about the question at all. Doubt is what faith feels like from the inside when it is alive and honest, the friction of a trusting mind that still has questions. The Bible is full of people who believed and doubted in the same breath, the father who cried out that he believed and asked for help with his unbelief in the same sentence, and Jesus did not rebuke him. He healed his son. A faith with no doubt in it is usually not a strong faith. It is an untested one, or a dishonest one. The presence of your questions is not evidence that you lack faith. It may be evidence that your faith is real enough to ask.

## The Gap Between Evidence and Commitment

Now let me concede the real difficulty, because there is one and the skeptic is right to press it. Even granting that faith is grounded trust rather than blind belief, faith does go beyond the evidence in a way ordinary knowledge does not. When you commit your life to God, you are not in the position of someone who has finished a proof. You are in the position of someone who has weighed the reasons, found them substantial but not coercive, and then committed. There is a gap between the evidence and the commitment, and faith lives in that gap. The skeptic says, fairly, that this gap is exactly the problem, that you should believe only as strongly as the evidence warrants and not one inch further, and that stepping past the evidence is the very irrationality being objected to.

Here is what I would say back, and it is the heart of the matter. That gap is not unique to religion. It is a feature of every important commitment a human being makes. The evidence that your spouse loves you does not amount to a mathematical proof, and it never will, and yet you marry, you commit, you build a life on a trust that outruns certainty, because some realities cannot be known in any other way. There are things you can only discover by committing to them first. You cannot know whether a friendship will hold by analyzing it from outside forever. At some point you have to extend trust, and only then does the deeper evidence arrive. The demand to wait for certainty before committing to anything is not a higher rationality. It is a recipe for a life in which you never marry, never trust, never love, because none of those things hands you proof in advance. Pascal saw that we are already committed, already wagering with our lives whether we like it or not, that there is no neutral spot to stand on where the question costs us nothing. To refuse to decide is itself a decision.

## The Obligations of Grounded Trust

So faith, rightly understood, is not believing without evidence. It is committing on the basis of evidence to a reality you cannot fully verify in advance, the way you commit to a person, the way you commit to anything that matters. It involves trust precisely because it involves a relationship, and relationships cannot be reduced to proofs without ceasing to be relationships. The Christian is not asked to switch off his mind. He is asked to do what every loving and trusting and committed person does, to lean his weight on something he has good reason to trust before he can see the whole of it.

> The only faith worth having is the kind that has looked, and asked, and is still willing to lean its weight.

There is one more thing worth saying, and it cuts the other way, against the comfortable believer rather than the skeptic. If faith is grounded trust, then it has obligations. It is not allowed to be lazy. A faith that refuses to examine its grounds, that treats every hard question as an attack, that prefers the warm feeling of certainty to the harder work of thinking, has betrayed its own nature. The tradition at its best has never been afraid of questions. It produced Augustine and Aquinas and the universities and centuries of argument, because it believed that all truth is God's truth and that an honest examination, followed all the way down, would not finally turn out to be its enemy. The person who is afraid to ask the hard questions does not have strong faith. He has a weak faith that he is protecting from exposure. Real faith can stand in the open air.

So I will leave you with the question turned around. You have been told that faith means believing without evidence, and now you have seen that this is not what faith has ever meant in its own tradition, that it means grounded trust extended into commitment, the same thing you already do in every relationship you have. The honest question, then, is not whether faith is irrational. It is whether the grounds are good. That is a question worth your full attention and your hardest scrutiny, and the tradition, at its best, does not fear that scrutiny. It invites it. The only faith worth having is the kind that has looked, and asked, and is still willing to lean its weight.

title: Why Would a Good God Allow So Much Evil?
excerpt: The suffering in the world is the oldest and heaviest reason to doubt God, and it deserves to be answered at full weight rather than waved away.
body:
This is the one that actually keeps people up at night.
