Not the clever objections, not the debates about miracles or morality, but the child with cancer, the village swallowed by the wave, the cruelty that lands on people who did nothing to deserve it. If God is all-powerful, He could stop it. If He is all-good, He would want to. It happens anyway, in oceans, every day. So either He cannot stop it, in which case He is not the God anyone means by the word, or He will not, in which case His goodness is a word that has lost its meaning. This is the problem of evil, and it is not a problem you solve. It is a wound you live with, and any answer that does not feel the wound is not an answer worth having.

## The Objection at Its Most Honest

Let me state it at its full and terrible strength, because the cheap versions of faith deserve to be broken against it. The argument is not improved by adding up the suffering, though the sheer quantity is staggering. It is sharpest at a single point. Take one child, one instance of innocent agony, the kind that does no one any good, that teaches no lesson, that simply destroys. The philosopher who pressed this hardest, building on Dostoevsky, said he would refuse a heaven built on the unavenged tears of one tortured child, would hand back the ticket. That is the objection at its most honest. It is not asking for a theory. It is holding up a single suffering face and asking how any good purpose could be worth that, and it is right to ask, and the believer who answers too quickly has not looked at the face.

## Why the Small Answers Fail

So I am not going to offer you the small answers, because they fail in front of that face. The answer that suffering builds character fails, because some suffering destroys character, breaks people past repair, and because no decent person would torture a child to improve him. The answer that it is all part of a plan we cannot see fails as comfort, even if it is true in some sense, because it asks the grieving to be consoled by a blueprint they are not allowed to read. The answer that everyone gets what they deserve fails most of all, because Jesus Himself flatly rejected it, when they asked him whose sin caused a man's blindness and he said neither this man nor his parents, and when he refused to read the people crushed by a falling tower as worse sinners than anyone else. The Bible does not teach that suffering is distributed according to desert. The book of Job exists precisely to destroy that idea, and God's final word in Job is not an explanation. It is His own overwhelming presence, and a long refusal to give Job the theory he demanded. That refusal is itself a clue, and I will come back to it.

## The Cost of a World That Can Love

> A world with creatures who can genuinely love is a world with creatures who can genuinely refuse, and you cannot have the one without the other, because love that cannot be withheld is not love but a mechanism.

What the tradition does offer is not a single answer but a few true things that, taken together, change the shape of the question without dissolving the pain. The first is about freedom. A world with creatures who can genuinely love is a world with creatures who can genuinely refuse, and you cannot have the one without the other, because love that cannot be withheld is not love but a mechanism. A great deal of the world's evil, by far the most of it, is the cost of that freedom, the wars and cruelties and betrayals that are human choices and not divine ones. God could prevent every evil by removing every freedom, by reducing us to puppets who cannot harm because we cannot act, but the price would be the destruction of the very thing that makes us capable of love, and a universe of safe puppets may be a worse universe than this one. That does not cover the cancer or the wave, the suffering no one chose, and I am not pretending it does. But it covers more than people think, once you count honestly how much of the world's agony is delivered by one human hand to another.

## The Limits of Our Vantage Point

The second true thing is harder and goes against the grain of how we frame the whole problem. The objection assumes that we are competent to judge, that if we cannot see a good reason for some suffering then there probably is none. But that assumption is doing enormous unnoticed work. To know that an instance of suffering serves no possible good purpose, you would have to see all of its consequences, down every branching path, across all of time, in every life it touches and every life those lives touch. No human being is in a position to make that judgment, and we know we are not, because we experience it constantly on a small scale. The pain that felt purely destructive at thirty turns out, at fifty, to have been the hinge everything good turned on, and we could not have seen it at the time. This does not mean all suffering has a hidden purpose we could endorse if we saw it. It means our inability to see a purpose is weak evidence that there is none, because our vantage point is so small. The argument from evil quietly requires us to be far more knowing than we are.

## A World That Groans

There is a third thing the tradition says, and it is the one most easily turned into a cruelty, so I will handle it carefully. Christianity claims that something went wrong with the world, that it is not now as it was made to be, that a rupture runs through the whole of creation and not only through human choices. This is not the claim that each sufferer deserves his suffering, which Jesus flatly denied. It is the larger claim that we live in a wounded world, a creation that the Bible describes as groaning, subjected to decay, waiting to be set right. On this view the cancer and the wave are not God's verdicts on particular people. They are symptoms of a deep disorder in the fabric of things, a brokenness that touches everything and falls, like rain, on the just and the unjust alike. This does not tell you why your child and not another, and I will not pretend it does. But it refuses the two cruelties that usually fill the silence, the cruelty of saying you must have deserved it and the cruelty of saying this is exactly how a good world should run. It says neither. It says the world is broken, that God knows it, and that He has not left it broken.

But I promised not to hide behind theory, and these two points, true as they are, remain theory, and theory does not weep. So let me tell you what is actually different about the Christian answer, because in the end it is not an argument at all. Every other system, when confronted with this, tries to explain suffering, to fit it into a scheme that makes it acceptable, to get God off the hook by giving you a reason. Christianity does something stranger and, I think, far more to the point. It does not finally explain suffering. It says that God entered it.

## The God Who Walked Into the Fire

> He is not the absent landlord of a burning house. He walked into the fire.

This is the center, and it is the thing the world's other answers do not have. The God of the Christians is not a distant being who arranged a world of pain and watches it from a place where pain cannot reach Him, handing down explanations from the safe seats. He came down into it. He took on a body that could be tortured and was. He was betrayed by a friend, abandoned by the rest, beaten, mocked, and nailed to a post to suffocate in public, and at the worst of it He cried out that even God had forsaken Him. Whatever you think happened on that cross, you cannot say that the Christian God does not know what suffering is from the inside. He is not the absent landlord of a burning house. He walked into the fire. The deepest answer Christianity gives to the problem of evil is not a sentence. It is a wounded man on a cross, and the claim that the man is God.

Why does this matter, if it does not stop the suffering. It matters because the real anguish of the problem of evil is not finally intellectual. It is the fear that the suffering means we are alone, that the universe is indifferent, that no one sees and no one cares and there is no one to cry to. The cross does not answer the question why. It answers the deeper question, the one underneath, which is whether we are alone in it. And the Christian answer is no. God is not the cause of your suffering held at a distance. He is the one who has joined you in it, who has been to the bottom of the worst of it before you, who meets you there not with a lecture but with His own scars. Dostoevsky's challenge, the unavenged tears of the child, gets its real answer not in a theory but in a person who took the tears of the world into Himself and answered them with His own blood.

## The Promise That It Will Be Undone

And there is the second half, without which the cross is only a tragedy. Christianity does not end at the suffering. It claims that the suffering was not the last word, that the tortured man walked out of the grave, and that this is the preview of what God intends for the whole groaning world. The promise is not that the suffering had a tidy purpose. The promise is that it will be undone, that there is coming a day when, as the old text says, He will wipe away every tear, when death itself dies, when the wave and the cancer and the cruelty are not merely explained but defeated and reversed. The Christian hope is not that the child's suffering will be justified by some greater good in the ledger. It is that the child will be raised, healed, made whole, and that the God who wept will set it right in a way that does not balance the books but breaks them, swallowing the evil in a flood of restored life. That is either true or it is not, and everything hangs on whether the tomb was empty. But if it is true, then the tears are not the end of the child's story, and the One who refuses, with Dostoevsky, to accept a heaven built on unavenged tears, turns out to agree with God, who did not accept it either, and did something about it at infinite cost to Himself.

> It is a God who came into it, who suffered it Himself, who promises to end it, and who asks you, in the meantime, not to understand but to trust

So I will not close this neatly, because the wound is still open and will be until that day. You will still stand at gravesides. The wave will still come. I have buried children and I have no formula that makes that bearable, and I distrust anyone who says he does. What I have, what the faith offers, is not an explanation that makes the suffering acceptable. It is a God who came into it, who suffered it Himself, who promises to end it, and who asks you, in the meantime, not to understand but to trust, the way Job finally trusted, not because he got his answer but because he met the One who was big enough to be trusted with the question. The problem of evil is the strongest case against God. It is also, in the strangest turn, the place where the Christian God comes closest, because He is the only God who has the wounds to show you. Whether that is enough is something you will have to decide standing where the suffering actually is, which is the only place the question was ever really asked.
